newsitem.title: FRANCE: Asterix enters museum, praised as modern myth.
newsitem.headline: Asterix enters museum, praised as modern myth.

text.p: Asterix the irrepressible Gaul and his anti-Roman resistance fighters became a museum exhibit on Monday, with a cabinet minister hailing the comic strip hero as a modern French myth.

"The Asterix Exhibition" at Paris's National Museum of Arts and Popular Traditions, which specialises in anthropology, dissects the lure of the cartoon which has sold more than 280 million books worldwide -- 100 million more than Tintin.
"Asterix has become a contemporary myth," Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy told a news conference.
"Asterix lives in an imaginary Gaul which looks more like modern France with its traffic jams, its political elections and its problems than the Gaul of Vercingetorix," Douste-Blazy said.

The exhibition is a blast of cultural pride for France, which seeks to limit Hollywood imports and where Mickey Mouse has set up a European home at the Disneyland Paris theme park. Hundreds of U.S. hamburger restaurants flourish in France.

The exhibition runs from October 30 to April 21 and will then travel to Montreal. "Strip cartoons are popular art," Douste-Blazy said. He denied he was seeking to promote the books: "Asterix and Obelix don't need the culture ministry."
"It's unheard of for a comic strip character to get into a national museum," said artist and author Albert Uderzo, who has written Asterix books alone since the death of writer Rene Goscinny in 1977.

He praised the exhibit, which combines real artefacts from ancient Gaul and Rome -- including a bust of emperor Julius Caesar, statues, cauldrons, nails and pottery -- with cartoon pictures of Asterix and friends.

It shows original 1959 sketches of the first Asterix and a slim version of his now rotund friend Obelix, twin heroes of the tales about a village resisting the Roman occupation in 50 B.C. with the help of a magic strength-giving potion.
It says the real Gauls, for instance, invented soap and washed their hair with lime to make the colour lighter.
And it allows the museum's anthropologists escapism from more dusty analysis. "Asterix functions as a myth in the classical sense of the term," said Frederic Maguet, one of the exhibit's organisers.

As a myth, Maguet said Asterix contained seeds of a founding story about France, that Asterix now belonged to readers more than his creators and that the works contained a timeless theme of a struggle against oppression.

The exhibits also light-heartedly tick off the books for getting facts wrong. It says the Gauls farmed cows, sheep and pigs and hunted hares, for instance, but did not catch wild boar with their bare hands as Asterix and Obelix do.
"If we'd made the true history of Gaul it wouldn't be very funny," Uderzo said. "We know the Gauls cut their enemies' heads off and put them on spikes. They didn't take prisoners."
But he added: "I will make sure I'm a bit more serious about my studies in future."
